messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rosa is a 59-year-old divorced physical therapist who grew up in a household where her mother’s rages were as unpredictable as they were brutal. She remembers one evening when she was eight: her mother had been drinking, and Rosa had left a single dish in the sink. The memory comes to her not as a story but as sudden fragments—the sound of glass breaking, the sting of a slap, her own small body pressed against the kitchen floor. Sometimes, when she recalls it, she feels nothing at all, as if she is watching a stranger in a film; at other times, the memory feels so extreme that she cannot quite believe it happened to her. These pieces surface without warning—while she is folding laundry, or in the middle of a patient’s rehabilitation session—and each time they do, Rosa’s chest tightens and her eyes dart to the door.

In the decades since, Rosa has built a life around avoiding anything that could feel stressful. She schedules her physical therapy appointments with rigid precision, leaving no gaps for unexpected conversations with colleagues. She has come to believe that strangers approaching her—even a patient who steps too close to adjust their brace—pose a threat she cannot name. At work, she always positions herself so that her back is against a wall, her eyes sweeping the room. At night, she wakes three or four times to check the locks, to listen for footsteps, to confirm that no one has entered. The cleaning began as a small habit—wiping down her treatment table between patients—but it has become something else: she now scrubs her kitchen counters for forty-five minutes each evening, reorganizing the spice rack until it feels right, because the act of controlling her environment is the only thing that quiets the alarm in her chest.

The connection between the memory fragments and her vigilance is something Rosa feels in her bones. When a flash of her mother’s face appears—sudden, unbidden—her body responds before her mind can catch up: her shoulders tense, her breathing quickens, and she scans the room for an exit. That sense of threat, in turn, drives her to clean more fiercely, to eat an entire bag of chips while standing at the counter, to double-check the locks again. And the more she engages in these routines, the more the memory surfaces: washing her hands for the third time might trigger the fragment of her mother’s hand raised mid-swing, and the cycle tightens.

A few months ago, Rosa found herself avoiding a particular patient—an older woman with a loud voice—because the sound triggered the sudden pieces of memory. She rescheduled the woman four times before her supervisor asked if something was wrong. Rosa said she was fine, but she knew she was not. What finally brought her to seek help was a night two weeks ago when she woke at 3 a.m., convinced she heard her mother’s footsteps in the hallway, and spent an hour scrubbing the bathroom floor on her hands and knees. She is most afraid that the fragments will keep coming, that the cleaning will take over her life completely, and that one day she will not be able to leave the house at all. She hopes, quietly, that someone can help her feel safe in her own skin.
